doc.title: Virginia Mayhew interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 23, 2022

chapter: Teaching and the state of jazz
title: Where she fits in today's jazz without swing and blues
summary: She feels today's jazz lacks swing and blues, discusses playing around the time with Rowe, and both lament players who sound alike after school.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: No. Never. But right now I’m not considering another profession, but I’m trying to figure out where I fit in today. Because jazz, the jazz of the people that are 40ish or maybe even 50ish, whenever the jazz schools really got going, the music they’re creating, and they’re fast becoming the majority if not already, it doesn’t have two of the things that I fell in love with jazz, the swing and the blues are pretty much missing. And I’m just trying to figure out where — I’m not going to change who I am or what I do, I’m always trying to grow. But I’m not sure where I’m going to fit in with where it’s going now.

You’re — it’s almost like you’re reading my thoughts here because I’ve been listening not as much as I should but I think what I’m confused about is the time — you know there’s a way to play the time and there’s a way to play around with the time. And many of the things I hear it’s like everybody in the rhythm section is playing around with the time. So where exactly is it? And I guess I’m an old fashioned groove guy. I need — I don’t want to think too hard to hear it.

Well it’s definitely a different thing. And basically I’m with you but I also love that, but not as a place to live. I like to visit there. And the better I’ve gotten at it the more fun it is. But I think it’s really — it depends on what music you’re playing. No that’s not true. I don’t know. I’m okay with it being more — less rigid. I’m okay with that. I love that too. But I think I know what you’re talking about and it’s a little too esoteric for you maybe. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

Yeah I think it is. I know that the musicians that I’ve interviewed that were playing in the 40s and 50s, they often would say, “Well today’s generation, they all sound the same. They get the books and they learn the licks and then they sound the same.”

I agree wholeheartedly. And I think that’s really what’s happening today. And there are some great musicians but I just don’t relate to it. And everybody below the great people, they all sound the same. They go to school and they all learn the same thing, and they all have — I mean this is a gross generalization but it seems like in general they have incredible technique but they don’t — just like I said in the beginning they don’t have swing and they don’t have any blues in their playing. And it’s all sort of what you’re talking about, sort of a little bit. It’s open. And I like it when it’s open but not all the time. What do you think? It’s an interesting question.

It’s an interesting question and I think it has to do partly with jazz, as it should be, as been anointed as an art form now and certainly it should be, and it’s embraced by academia, but the thing that happened in smoky night clubs —
They have no experience of that.
